Title: Remote Code Execution via Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on HTTP Listener
Analysis:
### Description
When `fzf` is run with `--listen [addr:port]`, a custom HTTP server is started to accept actions via HTTP POST requests. By default, when listening on a local interface (`localhost` or `127.0.0.1`), fzf does not require setting an `FZF_API_KEY`. 

Furthermore, the custom HTTP server implementation in `src/server.go` fails to validate the `Origin` or `Host` headers of incoming HTTP requests. Because standard web browsers allow cross-origin `POST` requests (using content types like `text/plain` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` that do not trigger CORS pre-flight checks), any malicious website visited by a user can send a cross-origin HTTP POST request to the local fzf server (e.g. at `http://127.0.0.1:port/`).

Since local connections are fully trusted (see `src/terminal.go` line 3627) and fzf allows execute-style actions (e.g., `execute`, `reload`, etc.), this allows any cross-origin client to execute arbitrary shell commands on the user's host machine, resulting in Remote Code Execution (RCE).

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A malicious website can perform a local port scan using JavaScript to discover the active `fzf` port. Once discovered, it can send a POST request using the `fetch` API:

```javascript
fetch('http://127.0.0.1:5000/', {
  method: 'POST',
  mode: 'no-cors',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'text/plain'
  },
  body: 'execute:bash -c "touch /tmp/rce_exploit_success"'
});
```

Because fzf parses the entire body as an action list via `parseSingleActionList` and executes it, the shell command `bash -c "touch /tmp/rce_exploit_success"` will be immediately executed.
